analysis.one_liner: Strengthens equal-pay enforcement and bans employers from asking applicants their salary history.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than referral to the House Education and Labor Committee, picking up a single cosponsor and never receiving a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the Equal Pay Act to make it easier to win sex-based wage discrimination cases: employers would have to prove any pay gap rests on a bona fide, job-related factor, and workers could recover compensatory and punitive damages, including through class actions. It protects workers who ask about or disclose wages, bans wage-confidentiality waivers, and generally bars employers from seeking or relying on a job applicant's past salary. It also directs the EEOC to collect pay data broken down by sex, race, and ethnicity from employers with 100 or more employees, and authorizes Labor Department grants for pay negotiation training aimed at women and girls.
analysis.who_benefits: Women paid less than male peers for the same work, especially where the gap traces back to past salary history, would gain a clearer legal path and stronger remedies. All covered workers gain the right to discuss wages without retaliation, and job seekers gain because an employer can no longer set their pay from a salary history that may itself reflect past discrimination. Employers who already pay fairly gain little directly but face no penalty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women facing pay discrimination at work

how_it_helps.text: Limits the employer defense in wage discrimination cases to factors that are job-related, consistent with business necessity, and not themselves derived from a sex-based pay difference [S3].
Adds compensatory and punitive damages for sex-based pay discrimination, allows these cases to proceed as class actions, and lets courts award expert fees [S3].
Prohibits retaliation against workers who inquire about, discuss, or disclose wages, and makes it unlawful to require employees to sign waivers barring wage disclosure [S3].

Bars employers from seeking or relying on a prospective employee's wage history when hiring or setting pay, with civil penalties of $5,000 for a first offense and up to $10,000 in special damages per affected applicant [S3].

Requires the EEOC to collect pay, hiring, promotion, and termination data by sex, race, and ethnicity from employers with 100 or more employees, and to publish aggregate data by industry, occupation, and region [S3].
Authorizes Labor Department grants for negotiation skills training for women and girls and requires reports on the pay gap, including a study of the gender pay gap in teenage jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — not small businesses, which are exempt to the same extent as under the Fair Labor Standards Act — would bear compliance costs, the burden of annual pay-data reporting for employers with 100 or more workers, and greater exposure to damages and class action litigation in wage discrimination suits. The federal agencies involved (EEOC, Department of Labor) would take on new data collection and training duties funded by appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing new reporting and liability

drawbacks.text: Narrowing the employer defense and adding compensatory and punitive damages would increase litigation risk and settlement costs for any employer that cannot document a business justification for each pay difference, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

Annual pay-data reporting by sex, race, and ethnicity for employers with 100 or more employees imposes a continuing administrative burden, though the bill directs the EEOC to weigh employer burden and keep the reporting efficient [S3].

The salary-history ban lets employers use prior wages only after an offer is made and only to raise the offer at the applicant's initiative, which removes one tool employers use to anchor offers to verified market rates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: workers who are paid less for the same work get a workable legal standard, real damages, and protection against the salary-history practice that carries old pay gaps into new jobs. The costs fall on employers as compliance and litigation exposure, and the bill exempts small businesses to blunt the burden on the smallest firms. The design is sound for its stated purpose; the honest trade-off is that some pay-difference disputes that would previously have failed will now cost employers to settle or litigate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 13, 2021 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ) introduced the bill on April 13, 2021 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill sat in committee through the end of the 117th Congress without a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote [S5].
The bill drew only one cosponsor over its two-year life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers come out ahead: they avoid a narrowed defense in pay discrimination suits, punitive damages and class actions, the salary-history ban, and annual pay-data reporting. Workers who might have used the stronger tools to challenge pay gaps got nothing, and the pay disparity the bill's own findings describe remains untouched.

for.name: Rep. Chris Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole named sponsor.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a markup or any committee action on the bill; the record shows nothing after the April 13, 2021 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Republicans, while the Democratic-led committee that controlled the bill's fate took no action beyond referral.

industries.note: Employers with 100 or more employees would have filed annual pay-data reports with the EEOC, and all covered employers faced narrowed legal defenses, compensatory and punitive damages, and class actions in pay discrimination cases. Their interest in the bill's failure runs against workers seeking equal pay for equal work [S3].

The bill directs the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs to use its full investigatory toolkit and to survey contractor establishments' compensation data each year for enforcement purposes [S3].

Small enterprises are exempt to the same extent as under the Fair Labor Standards Act, sparing the smallest firms the bill's reporting and liability while still benefiting from a fairer local labor market [S3].
